content: Begin by summarizing the key points from the previous slide, specifically focusing on what should not be said or done in the context of providing psychological first aid (PFA). Role Play: Ebola Communication (10 minutes) This role play exercise is designed to help participants practice providing PFA to individuals who may have Ebola and cannot be physically touched. Select 3–5 volunteers to participate in the role play in front of the group. Once the volunteers are chosen, explain that you will act as the nurse, and each volunteer will have one minute to offer support using effective communication strategies. The scenario involves a nurse who has been exposed to Ebola during their duties and may be infected. The nurse developed a fever earlier in the day, stopped their shift early, informed their supervisor, and is now awaiting further instructions. The nurse is understandably very upset. Volunteers must offer support while keeping their hands clasped behind their backs to avoid physical contact. Each volunteer will have one minute to provide emotional support and help calm the nurse. After each volunteer’s turn, provide feedback on what was helpful and suggest areas for improvement. Then, move on to the next volunteer. Discussion: Ebola Communication Role Play (10 minutes) Facilitate a group discussion about the role play and the challenges of providing support to individuals you cannot touch, approach closely, or comfort in traditional ways. Encourage participants to reflect on how they can communicate effectively and safely with individuals who may be ill or infected with Ebola. Discuss the importance of tone of voice, eye contact, choice of words, and attentiveness. For example, participants might say, Even though I cannot touch you, I care about how you are feeling. Psychological First Aid (PFA) Overview The core principles of PFA are Prepare, Look, Listen, and Link. These principles guide helpers in providing effective support during crises. Prepare Before entering an Ebola-related situation, take time to prepare by: Learning about Ebola from reliable sources, including updates on the local situation. Understanding what other agencies in the area are doing and where people can access information and services, including immediate medical care. Having contact information for mental health and psychosocial resources available for those needing additional emotional and social support. Look The Look principle involves assessing the situation before offering help. Key steps include: Checking for safety: Identify any dangers in the environment and ensure it is safe for you and others to be present. If the health status of the person is uncertain, take all necessary precautions to avoid disease transmission. Avoid physical contact with the person or their belongings. Identifying people with urgent basic needs: Look for individuals who may need food, clothing, or medical attention. Determine who is most at risk in the area, such as children left without supervision or individuals facing discrimination or violence. Recognizing serious distress reactions: Identify individuals who appear extremely upset, unresponsive, or in shock. Consider who may benefit from PFA and how best to assist them. Listen The Listen principle emphasizes the importance of active listening to understand the person’s situation and needs. Key elements include: Approaching people respectfully and introducing yourself by name and organization. Asking about their needs and concerns, even if some needs may seem obvious. Listening attentively with your eyes, ears, and heart to help the person feel calm and supported. Avoid pressuring the person to talk but being available if they wish to share their experiences. Offer reassurance and emotional support, such as singing, storytelling, or simply staying present to ease their fear. Link The Link principle focuses on helping individuals regain control of their situation by connecting them with resources and support. Key actions include: Assisting people in addressing basic needs and accessing services, such as food, water, or medical care. Helping them cope with problems using their own strengths and coping strategies. Providing accurate information and connecting them with loved ones and social support networks. Emphasizing that the helper’s role is not to solve all problems but to empower individuals to address their own needs with the necessary resources and support. Helping People in Distress When assisting individuals in distress, it is important to: Maintain a calm and soothing tone of voice. Use eye contact to convey attentiveness and care. Reassure the person that you are there to help and remind them they are safe, if true. For individuals feeling disconnected or overwhelmed, guide them to reconnect with their environment and themselves. Techniques include grounding exercises, such as feeling their feet on the floor, tapping their fingers, or focusing on their breathing. Most people will recover emotionally over time, especially if their basic needs are met and they receive support. However, those with severe or prolonged distress may require additional help beyond PFA. Ensure they are not left alone and refer them to mental health and psychosocial specialists in the area.
